summary: Defines the publication stream for RFCs coming from the Internet Research Task Force. Most documents will come from IRTF research groups and are expected to be published as Informational or Experimental. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5743 explains how an Internet Research Task Force document can be published in the RFC series. The process includes review and makes clear that an IRTF RFC is not an Internet standard.

subtitle: The review and publication path for documents in the Internet Research Task Force stream.

tldr.problem: The Internet Research Task Force needed a defined way to publish research documents in the RFC series with a clear IRTF label.
tldr.mechanism: A research group reviews its document, the Internet Research Steering Group reviews and approves it, the IESG checks for conflict with standards work, and the RFC Editor handles publication.
tldr.outcome: IRTF-stream RFCs are research publications, not candidates for Internet Standard status. This Informational RFC describes the stream process.

facts.label: Internet Standard status
facts.value: IRTF stream RFCs are not candidates

today: RFC 5743 is an Informational RFC published in December 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it defines the IRTF document stream process described in the text.

sections.title: The IRTF RFC Stream
sections.content:
The Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) carries out Internet-related research and development. RFC 5743 defines a publication path for documents from that work, especially documents produced by IRTF Research Groups. The RFC Editor is expected to publish most of these documents as Informational or Experimental RFCs.

The stream gives research publications an IRTF label and includes review before publication. The document says the process was revised after more than a year of experience and the handling of roughly a dozen documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Research groups in the IRTF can publish their work in the RFC series through a defined process. The publication keeps an IRTF label so readers can identify its source.

sections.title: Research Group Preparation
sections.content:
Before submission, the Research Group (RG) reviews the document's technical and editorial quality and agrees that it should be published. The abstract identifies the document as the group's work. Near the beginning, the document describes the level of support for publication and the breadth of review it received.

The document must make clear that it is not an IETF product and not a standard. If it describes an experimental protocol, it includes appropriate usage caveats. It should cite related research. The RG also names a document shepherd to track the work and help it move through publication.
sections.plainLanguage: The research group checks the document and explains how much support and review it received. The text must also say clearly that the work is research, not a standard.

sections.title: IRSG Review and IESG Review
sections.content:
The Internet Research Steering Group (IRSG) reviews and approves documents intended for the IRTF stream. Its review focuses on technical clarity, editorial quality, and whether the Research Group has reviewed the document adequately; it is not a deep technical review. At least one reviewer must not chair the Research Group. Reviews are public, and all comments must be considered, though the RG need not accept every suggestion.

After IRSG review, the IRTF Chair gives the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) an opportunity to review the document under RFC 5742. The IESG checks whether the Informational or Experimental designation is being used to bypass the Internet Standards Process. It normally responds within four weeks.
sections.plainLanguage: The IRSG checks whether the research document is clear and properly reviewed. The IESG then checks that its publication label does not disguise standards work.

sections.title: RFC Editor Handling
sections.content:
After the IESG review opportunity, the IRTF Chair asks the RFC Editor to publish the document. The document enters the RFC Editor queue at the same priority as non-standards-track IETF-stream and IAB-stream documents. The document shepherd helps the authors respond to editorial questions, including during the AUTH48 stage.

If needed, the RFC Editor adds the labels and status text identifying the publication as an IRTF document. The document is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, as the RFC's status text explains.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the review steps are complete, the IRTF Chair asks the RFC Editor to publish the document. The editor labels it as an IRTF publication, and it remains separate from Internet standards.

sections.title: Rights and Intellectual Property
sections.content:
The IRTF stream aims to let research have broad impact, so publication rights should generally permit republication with suitable credit. Contributors submit Internet-Drafts and grant rights described in RFC 5378. Unless the RFC says otherwise, readers may make derivative works with attribution. An author may request that derivative works not be allowed, but that request may need to be discussed with the IRTF Chair.

Contributors are expected to follow IETF procedures for disclosing known patent and trademark issues. The IRTF prefers terms that do not require fees and do not discriminate among users, but this RFC sets no specific licensing requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: The stream generally allows people to reuse research with attribution. Contributors must disclose known patent and trademark issues, while the RFC does not require one particular license.
